solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Dresses up rip-off politicians

indicators.note: Something off has gone out of its proper state, and letters out of their proper state are read in a new order.

parts.note: the three letters of rip, resettled
mps is the short form for members of parliament

explanation.surface: Politicians being smartened up for a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dresses up' looks like an instruction to tidy the letters and is the definition instead; the shuffling is done by the 'off' of 'rip-off'. A rip-off is a swindle, so the hyphenated word reads as one idea.
explanation.definitionFit: To primp is to fuss over your own appearance, adjusting clothes and hair, which is what dressing up amounts to.

clue.text: Outline plan for overseeing suspect movement

indicators.note: To oversee is to watch from above, so in a down entry the piece doing it sits on top of the rest.
Movement is letters shifting out of the places they were in, which leaves them standing in a different order.

parts.note: to be pro something is to be for it
the seven letters of suspect in another order

explanation.surface: A plan drawn up for keeping watch on some dubious activity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' looks like the adjective describing the movement and is the raw material instead. Pro for 'for' is the vote in favour, as in weighing the pros and cons.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospectus sets out in advance what a school or a share issue intends to do, which is an outline of the plan rather than the plan itself.

clue.text: Go along with eluding nuts

indicators.note: Someone nuts is out of their right mind, and letters sent out of their right order are what that produces here.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Agreeing to dodge the lunatics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' sits right beside the letters it stirs and reads as the people being dodged. To indulge somebody is to let them have their way, a softer thing than the surface's flight suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To indulge a person is to let them have their way rather than argue, which is going along with whatever they want.

clue.text: (& 15dn.) Prudish English members of the clergy: we've had too many in recent times

definitions.text: we've had too many in recent times
definitions.note: The definition identifies the answer by a complaint rather than a synonym: Britain ran through five holders of the office between 2016 and 2024, which is the grumble the setter is trading on.

parts.note: prim is the word for prudishly proper
e is the standard short form for English
a minister is a member of the clergy in the nonconformist churches

explanation.surface: Straitlaced English clergymen, of whom there have lately been far too many.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon does the work of a link word: everything before it builds, everything after it defines. Minister covers both the man in the pulpit and the man in the cabinet, which is what hides the join.
explanation.definitionFit: The grumble is about the churn at Number 10 — the country got through five holders of the office in eight years — so the complaint points straight at them.

clue.text: Instrument Starmer put back into firm Trumpian behind

indicators.note: into means the reversed letters go inside the rest

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm
ass is the American word for backside, as Trump would say

indicators.note: put back means set the other way round, so the two letters for the prime minister are reversed

parts.note: Keir Starmer is the PM, the UK Prime Minister

explanation.surface: A Private Eye jibe at Starmer pushed back into Trump's rear end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trumpian' marks the American spelling: ass rather than the British arse.
explanation.definitionFit: A compass is an instrument for finding direction, or a drawing instrument for circles.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) Mafia business, say — Eric M. as Cyclops might put it?

parts.note: for those five letters to work as a clue they need a word telling you to rearrange them, and the setter's way of putting it supplies one
the five letters of Eric M set down in another order

explanation.surface: A Mafia man — Eric M, say — named the way the setter would name him.
explanation.walkthrough: This one runs backwards: the answer is not built out of 'Eric M', it is the instruction that would clue 'Eric M'. Setters call that a reverse anagram. Cyclops is Private Eye's setter, so his way of putting a thing is a cryptic clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Rackets run as a standing business by a syndicate are what the phrase names, and 'say' admits the Mafia is one example of it rather than the whole.

clue.text: Lords member holds up no.1 trailblazer

indicators.note: To hold something is to keep it inside your grasp, so the word named first closes round the letters that follow.
A down entry is written from the top downwards, so letters told to come up are read from the foot of the column back to its head.

parts.note: a peer is a member of the House of Lords, Britain's unelected upper chamber
no and the figure one give NO and I, and the three letters are then read back up the column

explanation.surface: A member of the Lords holding up the number one record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No.1' reads as a chart-topper and is really two scraps of letters, the figure standing in for the letter i. 'Holds up' does two jobs at once, wrapping one piece and turning the other over.
explanation.definitionFit: A pioneer is the first to open new ground, and blazing a trail is cutting marks in trees so that others can follow the same route.

clue.text: Lawyer — southern kind

parts.note: s is the standard short form for southern
your ilk is your kind or sort

explanation.surface: A lawyer of a particular southern type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' is the noun and not the adjective, which is what makes a two-piece charade out of three words. The dash is Cyclops fencing the definition off from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Silk is what the English bar calls a senior barrister, from the silk gown worn once appointed King's Counsel.

clue.text: Some brandy for each kid?

parts.note: a nip is a small measure of spirits poured out
per is the Latin for each, as in miles per hour

explanation.surface: Brandy poured out for every child in the room.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark apologises for the surface, where the children are being handed spirits. Nipper is the British word for a small child, with nothing to do with drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Nipper is the affectionate British term for a young child, so 'kid' names the same small person in another register.

clue.text: Leaving without Dom, it's fantastic — just what the comedian needs

indicators.note: Without carries its older sense of outside, so the word before it goes round the letters that come next.

parts.note: leaving is going, and the word splits in two to make room

indicators.note: What is fantastic is wildly unlike the real thing, and letters made unlike themselves come out in another order.

parts.note: five letters from Dom and it, resettled in the gap; the 's is doing the work of 'is'

explanation.surface: A trip that only turns out brilliantly once Dom has been left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving without' looks like a deletion and is nothing of the kind — no letters go missing, one word merely opens up to admit another. Dom is Dominic Cummings, the adviser whose lockdown drive to Barnard Castle Private Eye never let go of.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedian lives or dies by landing the punchline at exactly the right moment, and that sense of the right moment is what the phrase names.

clue.text: Look round before getting leg over

indicators.note: In an across entry what comes before something else is written to its left, so the round letter leads.
Something sent over goes head over heels, so the letters it labels land in a different order.

parts.note: o is the round letter, the shape a nought makes
the three letters of leg, tipped into a new order

explanation.surface: Having a look about the place before getting lucky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leg over' is British slang for sex, which is why the surface reads as a night out rather than as three letters and a shuffle. The definition is the first word, standing alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to look at somebody with open lecherous interest, so 'look' is the plain verb sitting underneath the leer.

clue.text: Milky white colour of mobster after work?

indicators.note: In an across entry the piece that comes after another is written to its right, so the mobster's letters follow the work.

parts.note: op is the short form of opus, a composer's work
Al Capone is the crossword's standard mobster, known by his first name alone

explanation.surface: The shade a gangster turns once the job is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers a definition by example, since these stones come in fire reds and blues as well. Op is the abbreviation printed on a concert programme.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is the milky iridescent gemstone, pale enough that its name has been borrowed for the colour itself.

clue.text: Cost of Senate's final vote against "betrayer" of Trump, reportedly

indicators.note: To be up against a thing is to be right next to it, so this letter sits immediately in front of what follows.
The final of a word is the letter it ends on, so that one letter is all that comes across.

parts.note: the last letter of Senate
x is the cross a voter pencils into the box on a ballot paper

indicators.note: What is reported comes second-hand by word of mouth, so the piece is spelt as it sounds rather than as the name is written.

parts.note: Mike Pence was Trump's vice-president and refused to overturn the 2020 election result, which is what got him branded a traitor

explanation.surface: The bill for the Senate's last vote on the man who let Trump down.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks round 'betrayer' belong to Trump rather than the setter — they mark whose opinion it is. 'Vote' is the mark in the box, not a tally of ayes and noes.
explanation.definitionFit: An expense is a sum you have to lay out, so cost names the same money from the payer's side of the transaction.

clue.text: Mean — pissed on poor dears

indicators.note: In a down entry the thing sitting on another is above it, so the drunk word takes the top half of the column.
Poor work is badly done, and letters badly set down do not keep the order they came in.

parts.note: tight is one of the many British words for drunk, which is what pissed means here
the five letters of dears in another order

explanation.surface: A drunk relieving himself over some poor unfortunates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed on' invites the lavatorial reading and is really two instructions, one of them the direction down the column. In British use pissed means drunk, where American use has it meaning annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody tight-arsed will not part with a penny, and mean is the everyday British word for exactly that stinginess.

clue.text: Sun, low grade paper, comic

definitions.note: The definition names a funny person where the answer is the laughter they get: British usage calls anyone reliably hilarious a scream, so the reaction stands in for the performer.

parts.note: s is the standard short form for sun, as on a weather map
c is the low grade on a school report, sitting below a and b
a ream is the printer's bundle of five hundred sheets

explanation.surface: The Sun, a downmarket rag, read as a comic.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's standing view of the Sun is the joke, and the tabloid's name is doing duty as a single letter. The commas make one continuous sneer out of three separate scraps and a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything that leaves you helpless with laughter gets called a scream in British speech, the noise you make standing in for the funny thing itself.

clue.text: see 3dn.
Practice bondage and relax before shower?

indicators.note: In an across entry the piece that comes before another is written to its left, so the relaxing word leads.

parts.note: to rest is to relax
a shower is a brief fall of rain

explanation.surface: An evening of rope work and a lie-down before the weather turns.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags how far a jokey definition sits from a dictionary one. 'Shower' is the weather rather than the wash, which keeps the second half looking domestic.
explanation.definitionFit: Bondage means tying a partner up, and to restrain somebody is to hold them so they cannot move — the definition is that act at its kinkiest.

clue.text: You finally ousted one in south coast town for electioneering

definitions.note: The answer is plural in form but names a single activity, which is why a singular noun for that activity is allowed to define it.

indicators.note: Finally is at the end, so the letter wanted is the one the word finishes on.
In marks where the swap happens, inside the word named next rather than beside it.

parts.note: Hastings is the Sussex seaside town by which the Normans landed in 1066

indicators.note: To oust someone is to put them out of the place they held, and the letter named takes over that vacated place.

parts.note: the last letter of you
a is the article that stands for one, and it is the letter ousted

explanation.surface: A sitting member finally unseated in a town on the south coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a by-election result, and 'ousted one' reads as the member losing his seat rather than a letter losing its place. The hustings were literally the platform candidates stood on to speak.
explanation.definitionFit: The hustings are the platform and the public meetings of a campaign, so the word covers the whole business of canvassing for votes.

clue.text: A lot of which contributes to jam trade

definitions.text: A lot of which contributes to jam
definitions.meaning: the road sense: too much of it on one stretch is what brings everything to a standstill
the commercial sense, used as noun and verb of dealing in goods, especially the illicit kind

explanation.surface: The preserves business and what goes into making the jam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jam trade' reads as one phrase about preserves, and prising the two words apart is the whole move: the jam belongs to the first definition, the trade to the second. Trafficking in arms or drugs is where the commercial sense still lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Vehicles crowding one road are what causes the standstill, and to traffic in something is to deal in it: one word for the movement of cars and of goods.

clue.text: Tabloid determined the ending of enlightenment?

parts.note: the Sun is Britain's best-known tabloid newspaper
somebody set on a course is determined to follow it

explanation.surface: A tabloid deciding that the age of reason was over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ending of' looks like an instruction to take a last letter and is the definition doing its work: what ends at dusk is the daylight. The Enlightenment with a capital letter is the eighteenth-century age of reason, which is where the surface gets its sneer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunset is the moment the light goes, so enlightenment puns on illumination — the end of being lit rather than the end of reason.

clue.text: Hospital in drab surroundings that is subject to inflation

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause rather than a noun, describing the answer by what has to be done to it before use rather than naming it.

indicators.note: In puts the letter bodily inside the word that follows rather than beside it.
Surroundings are what lie all round a thing, so the drab word closes over that letter from both sides.

parts.note: dingy means drab and dirty-looking
h is the standard short form for hospital, as on a road sign

explanation.surface: A hospital standing in dismal grounds, with the bills going up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inflation' is the economic kind on the surface and the foot-pump kind in the answer. 'Drab surroundings' is one idea in the sentence and two instructions underneath it, the word and the wrapping.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubber dinghy is blown up before it goes anywhere near the water, so being subject to inflation is a plain account of how it is made ready.

clue.text: Negative place of work, end of line for party candidate?

parts.note: no is the plain negative answer
a mine is the place where the work is done underground

indicators.note: The end of a word is the letter it stops on, so only that letter comes across.

parts.note: the last letter of line

explanation.surface: A gloomy verdict on a workplace at the end of the line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place of work' is the pit, one of the crossword's steady stand-bys, and it sits beside the letters rather than round them. The question mark admits that a nominee need not be political at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominee is the person a party formally puts forward to stand at an election, which is what being its candidate consists of.

clue.text: Almost pleasant to go after git? It could be the death of you

definitions.text: It could be the death of you
definitions.note: The definition warns about the answer instead of naming it: the setter gives the consequence rather than a synonym, which is how a poison gets defined without the word poison.

indicators.note: Almost a word is the word one letter short of finished, so its last letter never arrives.
What goes after something is written behind it, so these letters follow the ones already down.

parts.note: calling a man an arse is the same insult as calling him a git
pleasant is nice, docked of its last letter

explanation.surface: Going for an idiot would be almost enjoyable, and quite possibly fatal.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words for the fool are mild British abuse, which is why the swap reads so naturally in the sentence. The question mark covers a definition that warns rather than defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenic is the classic Victorian poison, tasteless in food and lethal in small doses, so a warning about dying picks it out exactly.

clue.text: see 5dn.
Drink, one's into the drink

indicators.note: Into means right inside, so the letter named goes in among the letters that follow.

parts.note: the drink is sailors' slang for the sea, and the Med is the Mediterranean, the sea the British holiday on
a stands for one, as in a dozen

explanation.surface: A drinker who has ended up overboard in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The drink appears twice and means something different each time: the definition wants a glass, the wordplay wants the sea. Mead is the honey wine the Anglo-Saxons drank from horns.
explanation.definitionFit: Mead is fermented honey, the oldest alcoholic drink brewed in Britain, so 'Drink' names the class of thing it belongs to.

clue.text: Issue can be avoided by its use?

definitions.meaning: read as the surface wants it, a problem or a matter that has to be dealt with

definitions.text: can be avoided by its use?
definitions.meaning: read the other way, where issue means offspring and the thing described is what stops them arriving

explanation.surface: A difficulty that can be sidestepped if you use the right thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Issue in the legal sense means offspring — 'died without issue' is the phrase out of a will — and the clue turns entirely on that older meaning. There are no letters to find here, only the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight as an account of contraception: the thing swallowed daily so that no children arrive.

clue.text: Barney is in fact iffy

indicators.note: In says the letters are sitting inside the words that follow, in the order they already stand.

parts.note: the run starts on the last letter of fact and carries straight into iffy

explanation.surface: A man called Barney who is, in truth, a bit dodgy.
explanation.walkthrough: Barney is British slang for a noisy row, not the name the capital letter makes it look like. 'In fact' reads as one phrase while only the 'in' is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A barney is a loud quarrel in British slang, the same sort of falling-out a tiff names, if a noisier one.

clue.text: Head of the Sweeney is, perversely, one who looked on as crime was committed?

definitions.text: one who looked on as crime was committed?

indicators.note: What is done perversely is done contrary to how it should be, and letters treated that way come out in the wrong order.
The head of a word is the letter at its front, so only that one letter is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of the word the
anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: The man in charge of the Flying Squad turning awkward about somebody who saw it all.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sweeney is the Metropolitan Police's Flying Squad — Sweeney Todd, rhyming slang for Flying Squad — and the 1970s television series named after it. 'Head of the' is a first letter, not the officer at the top.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyewitness is somebody who saw the thing happen with their own eyes, which is exactly what looking on while it was done amounts to.

clue.text: Sugar company's in fix

indicators.note: In puts the letters just named inside the word that follows.

parts.note: to glue something is to fix it in place
co is the short form of company, and the apostrophe-s brings an s along with it

explanation.surface: A sugar company that has got itself into difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In fix' is not quite idiomatic English, and that awkwardness is the tell: 'in' is the instruction rather than part of a phrase. 'Fix' is the verb to fasten, not the noun for a scrape.
explanation.definitionFit: Glucose is the simple sugar found in fruit and carried in the blood, so 'Sugar' names what it is rather than describing it.

clue.text: Foot, you might say, is a venerated person

indicators.note: Saying it aloud is the invitation to run the two pieces together, at which point the gap between them stops being audible.

parts.note: a foot hangs off the limb above it, and that limb is the first piece
and a foot is where that limb finishes, which is the second piece

explanation.surface: Michael Foot held up as a man to be revered.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter pulls in Michael Foot, Labour's leader in the early 1980s, when the clue wants the thing on the end of your leg. Run the two pieces together and the join between them disappears into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A legend is somebody spoken of with awe well beyond their actual deeds, which is what venerating a person amounts to.
